description: Starbyte Crew is a family team united by our love of space, astronomy, coding, and video games. We love exploring big ideas, building fun things, and learning how technology can help us understand the universe. For us, hacking is an adventure: we code, we explore, we play, and we have fun together.
summary:
Mars: Watney's Outpost is a web browser game in which students keep a fledgling Martian base alive. Power, water, oxygen, food and radiation shielding form one interdependent loop, and the planet tests it relentlessly: nightfall starves the solar arrays, dust storms dim the Sun, flares spike the radiation, and the pre-dawn cold freezes anything that loses its heater. An eight-mission campaign isolates one real engineering trade-off at a time, from storing energy for the night and mining ice rather than shipping water, to extracting oxygen from the thin carbon dioxide atmosphere, as NASA's MOXIE did, turning to nuclear power when dust blots out the Sun, keeping the outpost warm through a polar winter night, and shielding a crew whose radiation dose never heals. The final mission demands all of them at once.

Students don't read about these trade-offs; they live through them. An all-solar base goes dark at midnight, the water pumps stall, and the oxygen begins to fall. Every defeat ends in a debrief that names the cause and suggests a fix, so failure becomes the lesson rather than a dead end. The numbers are simple enough for a young player, but the relationships between them are real and traced to actual NASA missions, which makes every decision a genuine engineering decision. What students take away is an intuition textbooks struggle to convey: on Mars nothing comes free, and every choice costs something else.
details:
Mars: Watney's Outpost

A browser game about running a Mars outpost and making engineering trade-offs that decide whether a mission succeeds or fails.

Play: astro-game-lab.github.io/mars-watneys-outpost

30-second demo: Demo Video

Source code: github.com/astro-game-lab/mars-watneys-outpost

Running the outpost

Mars: Watney's Outpost puts students in command of a small research outpost on the Martian surface, with a single job: keep the crew alive long enough to make the trip worthwhile. The outpost runs on a closed loop. Power drives everything. Water is drawn from the ground. Habitats split it into oxygen, and Oxygen Plants extract more from the carbon dioxide atmosphere. Greenhouses turn water, power and heat into food, Mines supply building materials, and Science Labs earn the credits that pay for expansion. Every building on the hex map feeds one part of the loop and drains another, and the HUD shows each resource's net rate and how long it will last, so the consequence of every decision is visible within seconds.

Mars, meanwhile, keeps pulling at the loop. Each 120-second sol brings morning, midday, evening and a long night with no solar power at all. Dust settles on the panels until someone cleans them, dust storms cut solar output by seventy per cent, solar flares spike the radiation, micrometeorites knock buildings offline and pumps fail. The cold before dawn freezes any building whose heater loses power: a frozen Greenhouse loses its crop, a cold Lab stops working, and crew sleeping in a cold Habitat get hurt.

What follows are genuine engineering trade-offs. When power or water runs short, buildings are served by priority, life support first and science last, and the player can reorder them or switch buildings off to carry the batteries through the night. Keep the Lab earning, or keep the Greenhouse warm? The crew must raise every structure, repair every strike, clean every panel and pile regolith onto every shielded building, one job at a time, so a larger crew brings more hands but also more mouths and more lungs. Radiation is the slowest trade-off of all. Each astronaut carries a personal lifetime dose that never heals, lowers their maximum health, and sends them home at NASA's career limit. Shielding that arrives late arrives too late.

All of it is narrated by Mark Watney, in an unofficial fan work, whose dry humor turns warnings into jokes and briefings into stories. The tone stays light while the systems underneath stay serious.

One lesson per mission

The campaign is the tutorial. Each mission isolates a single piece of Mars engineering, opens with a briefing in Watney's voice that explains the science, and is deliberately built so that the obvious but wrong strategy fails for a real physical reason. Automated tests hold it to that: for every mission, the warned-against build order loses and a sound one wins.

1.   First Night: energy storage. An all-solar base blacks out after sunset.

2.   Ice Line: water comes from the ground, not from Earth. The ice lies beyond a ridge, and the water target is out of reach without it.

3.   Thin Air: oxygen from the carbon dioxide atmosphere, as MOXIE showed. Greenhouses alone cannot make enough air for a growing crew.

4.   Dust Season: nuclear power. Through near-constant storms, the best solar-only base reaches about a quarter of its target.

5.   Long Night: heating through a polar winter night, down to −113 °C. Weak winter sunlight cannot keep the outpost warm.

6.   Flare Watch: radiation shielding and cumulative dose. Shielding built after the flare comes too late.

7.   Crew Rotation: life support for a growing crew. A lander arrives every sol, and life support sized for a small crew falls behind.

8.   The Outpost: everything at once, on a fresh random map. Neglecting any single system ends the mission.

Winning the campaign unlocks the Hard and Martian tiers, which raise the crew's consumption, cut starting supplies and bring events more often, while keeping every mission winnable.

Learning from failure

Most space content tells students that Mars is hard. This game lets them discover it. A student who builds an all-solar base watches the batteries drain at midnight, the water pumps stall and the oxygen begin to fall. The debrief that follows names exactly what went wrong, whether that is who died, which need did the most harm and when it first ran out, or which objectives were left unmet, and suggests what to try next. The second attempt has a Battery Bank in it, or a Nuclear Generator, and the student understands why.

The explanations are there for anyone who wants them. Every building's "Why?" panel gives the real reason it exists and ties it to an actual mission: the dust that ended InSight, the 2018 storm that silenced Opportunity, the gusts and dust devils that swept Spirit's panels clean, the ice Phoenix dug up, the oxygen MOXIE made on Perseverance, and NASA's Kilopower fission test. For players who skip the reading, Watney offers brief tips at teachable moments, such as ice within reach, batteries that won't last the night or a Greenhouse heading for frost, each shown at most once a mission.

Honest by design

Space-themed STEM content tends to fail in one of two ways: it oversimplifies, or it buries a young learner in complexity. We avoided both by drawing a firm line between what the game claims about Mars and what it simplifies to stay playable. The relationships are claims, and they are true: solar fails at night and in storms, water comes from ice, regolith blocks radiation, and dose accumulates over a career. The numbers are a game economy, with a two-minute day and abstract resource units small enough for a young player to reason about.

Every factual statement the game makes to the player is listed in the project's physics document alongside its source, from NASA fact sheets and JPL mission reports to the NASA-STD-3001 radiation standard and peer-reviewed measurements from Curiosity's radiation detector. Every simplification is listed there too. A teacher can see exactly what is real and what is a game rule, and nothing the game teaches has to be unlearned later.

Built for the classroom

Schools have locked-down computers, tight budgets and short lessons, and the game is designed around all three. It runs in any modern browser from a single link, with no installation, account, plug-in, payment or advertising, and it collects no personal data; progress is simply saved in the browser. Missions last from a few minutes to about a quarter of an hour, with 2× and 4× speed, and an intro screen explains the whole loop in four cards, so no prior knowledge is assumed.

The simulation is also fully deterministic: the same seed and the same moves always produce the same outcome. The seed appears on the end screen, and adding ?seed=N to the link replays that exact Mars, so a whole class can face the same map and compare strategies, or a teacher can set a challenge such as surviving a particular seed. Because the code is MIT-licensed and the original art is released under CC BY 4.0, schools, clubs and other developers are free to use, translate and extend it.

What students take away

We want students to finish the campaign able to explain, in their own words, why a Mars base needs energy storage or nuclear power, why water is mined there rather than shipped from Earth, how astronauts can make oxygen from the Martian air, and why habitats are buried and radiation is treated as a career-long budget. Above all, we want them to carry away the idea that separates a space-themed game from a game about space engineering: on a real mission nothing comes free, and every choice costs something else.

Along the way, they meet the same constraints mission planners face, make trade-offs under pressure, fail, understand why, and try again. We hope that experience sends them looking for the real missions the game draws on, and towards the engineering careers that solve these problems for real.

Under the hood

1.   Technology platform: plain JavaScript, HTML5 and CSS, with no framework and no build step. The repository itself is the website. Code and images were generated largely by Claude Code Opus 5.5.

2.   Graphics: HTML5 Canvas 2-D for the hex map, with an off-screen cached layer for performance, hand-drawn SVG building sprites, and a public domain image of the Martian surface as the backdrop.

3.   Simulation: a custom deterministic engine, with a seeded random number generator (mulberry32), a fixed 0.05-second timestep independent of the frame rate, and resource flows resolved by priority tier.

4.   Testing: Node.js's built-in test runner, covering determinism, resource bookkeeping, shortages, connectivity, crew, temperature, events and the interface's text, plus a bot that plays every mission at every difficulty from scripted build orders.

5.   Hosting: GitHub for source control and GitHub Pages to publish the game.

6.   Science sources: NASA and JPL mission reports and fact sheets, NASA-STD-3001 for radiation limits, Curiosity RAD measurements (Hassler et al., 2014), and peer-reviewed papers on dust accumulation and Martian constants.

8.   Hardware: none required. The game runs on any computer with a modern browser.
